answer.exemplar: The opportunity cost of a tractor is the output of other goods that the same resources would have produced instead, expressed in units of one chosen good, usually grain. It is a rate of sacrifice rather than a cash cost, so it is found by setting the two output maxima against each other. If a country's resources make 90 tonnes of grain or 450 tractors in a year, then the 450 tractors stand for those 90 tonnes, and the cost of one tractor is 90 divided by 450, or 0.2 tonnes of grain. The figure matters because it is the price below which buying a tractor abroad is a bargain: a foreign supplier who offers one tractor for less than 0.2 tonnes of grain is cheaper than home production, and one who demands more is dearer. The number is also comparative. Two countries can have wildly different money costs for the same tractor and still trade, because what governs the trade is how much of each country's own forgone output the deal costs.

questions.explanation: An opportunity cost is a rate of sacrifice expressed in one good, and it is the pivot on which every trade claim turns. The explanation has to cover both halves of the idea: that it measures forgone output rather than money spent, and that it is obtained by dividing one output maximum by the other. What makes the concept worth teaching is that the same figure answers a decision question. It sets the price below which importing is worthwhile, and it is the basis on which two countries compare costs without moving any money. Students who treat it as a cash cost end up confused by a country that produces expensively and yet exports, which is only possible because the comparison is between forgone quantities of different goods rather than between bills in money. The second trap is quoting the ratio without saying which way round it runs, since 2.5 tractors per tonne and 0.4 tonnes per tractor are the same fact in opposite directions.

questions.explanation: A tariff is a tax at the border, so it raises the price paid inside the country and is collected by the state on the volume that still crosses. That gives the treasury a revenue line, but it also gives local users a higher price, and the two together are a transfer from users to the state rather than a gain. What is destroyed rather than transferred is the trade that no longer happens: production that would have been cheaper abroad is now made at home at a higher cost, and consumption that would have been worthwhile abroad is now priced out. Those two lost wedges are the deadweight loss, and they are the reason a tariff that raises revenue can still leave the country worse off. The tempting belief is that a tax collected domestically is a net addition to national income, which would make any tariff self-financing and self-improving. The other persistent error is assuming the exporter must absorb the price rise, when it is the home buyer who pays it unless the foreign side cuts its own price.

Under a floating rate the currency moves when the terms of trade or the flow of money changes, so the shock is spread across exporters, importers and savers rather than concentrated in employment. answer.exemplar: A floating rate is a shock absorber because the currency itself takes part of the adjustment. If world prices for a country's main export fall by a fifth, a floating rate lets the currency fall with them, so the domestic price of exports in home money is largely unchanged and the shock reaches wages and profits gradually through a longer period. A fixed rate forbids that move, because the rate is an announcement and the central bank has to buy and sell currency to hold it. The shock then has to be absorbed by something else. Interest rates may rise to defend the currency, which slows investment and spending; wages and prices may have to fall faster than they otherwise would, which is painful and slow; or reserves may be spent, which works only until they run out. What replaces the flexibility is therefore a choice of who pays: lenders, savers, workers or the central bank's reserve, and the choice is made by whoever holds the key to the currency.

questions.explanation: The point to establish is that flexibility is not a bonus but the mechanism, and a fixed rate is a promise that has to be paid for out of some other account. A floating rate lets the price of the currency do the adjusting, so a fall in export earnings is spread thinly across several years and across many kinds of income. Once the rate is fixed, that adjustment has to occur somewhere visible and somewhere soon, and the three usual candidates are interest rates, domestic prices and reserves, each of which carries a cost that the currency market would otherwise have absorbed. The explanation is incomplete without saying what replaces the flexibility, because a rate fixed through an indefinitely adjustable interest rate is not free stability. The tempting version of the argument claims a fixed rate avoids shocks altogether, when it removes the general-purpose absorber and leaves only the specific ones, which have to be used up and can run out.
questions.hint: Ask what takes the shock once the currency is no longer allowed to move.

questions.explanation: A terms-of-trade improvement is a real transfer, not a gain that appears from nowhere. The country can now buy more foreign goods with the same quantity of its own exports, so something has to have been given up elsewhere, and the counterpart is found in the rest of the world. Inside the country the same event is a redistribution rather than a net gain: the sectors producing exports earn more, and the households and firms buying imported goods and food pay more for what they buy. A fall in the price of food for consumers would require the import price to have fallen, and the whole point of the item is that it did not. The tempting belief that both sides gain treats a transfer as a creation, which is how a terms-of-trade improvement gets double-counted in a national accounts table. questions.explanation: The dividing line is control, not size or nationality. questions.explanation: A value chain is a set of stages in which the price of the finished good is divided, and the division follows how hard each stage is to replace. Design, brands and control of the specification are scarce: a buyer who wants a different product must go elsewhere and wait, so the holder of that stage can hold out for a larger share. answer.exemplar: Identical inputs do not guarantee identical outputs, because an indicator also contains a decision about which quantity to divide by, how to weight the parts, and how to combine them. A per-head measure and a total measure use the same population and income but divide and multiply by that population in opposite directions, so the country that is poorer per person can rank first on the total. Two composite scores built from the same components can still differ if one combines them by adding while the other takes a geometric mean, because the geometric mean punishes a low component far more severely than a simple average does. A third source of divergence is the choice of scale: a component capped at a ceiling compresses differences among countries that have already passed the cap, so a very high score can hide a large gap. answer.exemplar: The dependency ratio is a division, not a job. A ratio of dependants to working-age people can fall because the number of dependants has genuinely shrunk, through lower fertility and longer survival, and that is the change the dividend is supposed to reward. But a ratio is silent about what the growing working-age population is doing. If the country has no work for them, the dividend does not arrive: the additional people are supported by the same output, the extra labour supply is unemployed or underemployed, and wages are set by the scarcity of jobs rather than by the abundance of workers. A falling ratio can therefore coincide with rising unemployment, with falling wages, or with heavy outward migration, and in each case the country pays the cost of the extra mouths without receiving the benefit of the extra hands. What the ratio has to be joined with is an employment series, so that the additional working-age people can be shown entering productive work, and only then does the arithmetic of fewer dependants per worker become a rise in output per person. The dividend is a statement about employment, and a ratio is a statement about age.

questions.explanation: A claim that a project raised incomes is a causal claim, and causality needs a comparison against what would have happened without the project. Incomes per person have to be measured in settlements along the route and in settlements comparable to them but not on it, over the same years, so that a regional recovery or a general price rise cannot be read as the road's doing. The other options each produce a figure that could be true while the income claim was false. Traffic can be heavy while the route's households earn no more, the unit cost of a road is a budget measure with no behavioural content, and the split between public and donor funding says who paid rather than what was bought. This is the same requirement that applies to a special economic zone, where the missing piece is a comparison group rather than a bigger headline.
questions.hint: The claim is causal, so it needs a comparison with places the road did not reach.
questions.learningObjective: pair an income claim about a project with the measure that tests it

answer.exemplar: A remittance is a transfer of earnings from labour sold outside the country to the household left behind, and it arrives as income without passing through any domestic productive activity. The receiving household can spend it on food, school fees or a roof, so the effect on that household is immediate and large in proportion to its income. The country's production is untouched because the money was earned abroad, on a foreign employer, and the spending that follows is consumption rather than investment in a domestic plant, a workshop or a new crop. Spending of that kind may also raise prices in the receiving region, which transfers part of the gain to local producers without adding capacity. What would change production is a change in what the money is used for, or an effect on the labour market at home such as wages rising because fewer people are available to work locally, and neither follows from the transfer itself. So the right conclusion is narrow: remittances are a substantial and reliable income source whose developmental value depends on use, not a substitute for domestic investment.

questions.explanation: The distinction that has to be drawn is between a flow of income and a change in the capacity to produce. A remittance enlarges the household's budget without any domestic output behind it, so the living standard of that household rises at once. It leaves the structure of production alone because the labour was sold abroad, the employer is foreign, and the spending that follows buys consumption rather than adding to the stock of domestic productive capacity. What can change is the local price of things the household buys, and where local firms supply those goods some of the transfer stays in the local economy as extra turnover, but that is a distribution effect rather than an addition to capacity. The useful conclusion is conditional rather than dismissive: the developmental value of a remittance stream depends on what it is spent on, and on whether the absence of the migrant changes wages and demand at home. The tempting error is to treat a large inflow as self-financing growth.
questions.hint: Ask whether the money passes through any domestic production on its way to the household.
questions.learningObjective: explain why remittances raise incomes without changing production

questions.explanation: A cheaper seller abroad does not by itself make a home producer uncompetitive, because the comparison that matters is not the money price but the rate at which each side gives up its other output. What makes the withdrawal claim assessable is naming that ratio for both countries and asking which is lower. A partner can sell a good more cheaply in money terms and still give up more to make it, in which case specialising against it raises the country's own cost. The reverse case is the one where the minister is right, and the ratio is what distinguishes them. The other options each confuse cost with something correlated with it: wages are one input, export volume reflects history rather than cost, and a share of world output measures scale. None of the three would change if the two countries had identical costs and different sizes.
questions.hint: Money prices are not the comparison; forgone output is.
questions.learningObjective: pair a withdrawal-from-production claim with the measure that tests it

questions.explanation: A claim about self-financed growth is a claim about where the money that funds investment comes from, so the indicator has to measure that. The share of national saving supplied by remittances answers it directly: if a large part of the country's saving arrives as a private transfer from work done abroad, then the growth being described is being financed by an external flow, whatever the domestic saving rate looks like. The proportion of saving that is external, set against the investment it has to cover, is the figure that can defeat the claim, and it is the one the minister's statement cannot survive. The other options substitute a price for a flow, deny a link between the budget and external receipts that plainly exists, and confuse two distinct external receipts. A related error to watch for is counting the remittance as domestic saving, which would make the claim true by definition.
questions.hint: Ask where the saving that funds the investment actually comes from.

answer.exemplar: A region gains from trade when the terms on which it exchanges are better than the terms on which it could produce everything for itself, and that is a statement about the ratio of forgone output rather than about wages. If the region can produce food cheaply and the core can produce equipment cheaply, each side buys from the side that gives up less in making the good, and both end up holding more of both goods than either could produce alone. The real income gain is that the region is now using some of its labour in an activity at which it is relatively efficient instead of importing that good at its own high cost. Three things have to hold. The price the core pays must be above the region's own cost of making the good, or the region would be better off at home. The core's supply of finance and technology must be something the region cannot produce for itself at a lower cost, or there would be no trade at all. And the gains must be spent rather than absorbed by a rising rent of land and wages, since those can rise until the region's real position is much as it was. A structural argument about this exchange is a statement about how the gains are distributed, and it can be true of an exchange that is beneficial in total.

questions.explanation: The argument has to make clear that an unequal distribution of gains is not the same as a loss, and that the region can gain from an exchange it gets a small share of. The mechanism is comparative cost applied to two places: each buys from the producer that sacrifices least, and total output of the two goods rises. The conditions then do real work in the explanation, because they say what would have to change for the region to lose. If the price falls to the region's own cost, there is no gain. If the core's goods are ones the region can make as cheaply, there is no trade to begin with. And if the gains are competed away into land prices and wages, the region ends up with the same real income and a changed structure, which is the outcome a structural account is usually pointing at. The tempting error is to confuse a small share of a growing pie with a worse position, which makes every gain look like a loss.
questions.hint: The region's gain comes from buying what the core makes more cheaply than it can.
questions.learningObjective: state the conditions under which an unequal exchange benefits both sides

questions.explanation: The chain starts with the rate itself, because until it moves there is nothing for anybody to respond to. Once it has moved, the two price lists have both shifted in opposite directions, and that is what sets the conditions for the next step. Volumes follow, and they follow slowly, because a buyer who has signed a contract at the old price honours it, and a firm which has already ordered a year of inputs works through them. Only after the volumes have responded does the trade balance move, and it can move the wrong way at first, which is why the last step has to carry a qualification rather than a bare improvement. The step that is easiest to skip is the second, because a depreciation looks like an automatic competitiveness gain; it is not one unless exporters pass the fall on in the price rather than keeping it, and that is exactly the step the pass-through debate is about.
questions.hint: The rate moves first, prices follow, then volumes, and the balance last of all.
questions.learningObjective: sequence the transmission from a depreciation to a trade balance
